claim: Raven-style difficulty is driven by rule type, number of distinct rules and layout; a small rule taxonomy (constant, progression, add/subtract, distribute-3, XOR/logic) explains much of human item accuracy (rule-token count 57% of variance) and the same drivers shape LLM accuracy.
agent_test: Tag each test item by rule type and count; check agent accuracy falls with the same features at equal tokens; use as S0 difficulty features.

claim: Original RAVEN answer sets leak the answer: a context-blind model beats real models (ResNet 71.9% vs 53.4%; CoPINet 94.2%) and falls to chance on I-RAVEN (12.2%, 14.2%). Raven-type scores need a context-blind control.
agent_test: Run an options-only control on our items; discard items where it beats chance.

claim: Explicit perceive-then-induce-rule-then-execute pipelines (PrAE, NVSA) beat monolithic networks and stay robust where networks are not; this matches the constructive-matching account.
agent_test: Compare an agent forced to state the rule and expected cell before seeing options vs options-first, equal tokens.

claim: Perception is the main bottleneck for multimodal LLMs on matrix tasks: near chance on visual matrices (IQ50, RAVEN-S, MARVEL 25.7% vs humans 68.9%, MM-IQ best 33% vs 51%, MaRs-VQA open models 17-24%), while text or attribute input is far easier.
agent_test: Give text grids or attribute lists vs images on the same items; measure the gap; add a describe-first step.

claim: With attributes given as text, strong LLMs solve many Raven items (GPT-3 up to 93% on RAVEN 3x3Grid with naming plus decomposition; GPT-4 91-93% with per-attribute queries; GPT-3 beats students on Digit Matrices) but arithmetic rules and larger value ranges break them.
agent_test: Compare joint vs per-attribute prompts on arithmetic-rule items at equal tokens.

claim: Splitting a matrix problem into one query per attribute raises accuracy markedly (GPT-4 arithmetic rule 27.1% to 73.6%; OPT 1.3B 20-30% to over 70%).
agent_test: A/B joint vs disentangled prompt on the same items, equal total tokens.

claim: Reasoning models collapse under combined perceptual stress: o3-mini 81.0% to 17.0% and R1 82.8% to 23.2% on I-RAVEN-X at range 1000 when 10 confounders and smoothed values (pL=0.51) are combined (the often quoted 86.6% baseline is a different, easier setting). Each stress alone costs far less (o3-mini 69.8% with confounders, 75.6% with smoothing). High effort gave only 31.0% at 53,596 tokens.
agent_test: Add confounder attributes and fuzzy values to our items; check whether the agent keeps several candidate rules alive.

claim: Generic chain-of-thought does not reliably help on Raven text tasks (GPT-4 MC 0.697 to 0.596; open 0.410 to 0.385), and turning reasoning off helped 8-choice text Raven for some models; structured multi-round elimination did better (GPT-4o MaRs-VQA 33.96 to 41.96%).
agent_test: Compare plain CoT, hide-options constructive step, and multi-round elimination at equal tokens.

claim: Hypothesis-then-execute (System 2) prompting helps multiple-choice symbolic RAVEN (+31.9% relative) but hurts free generation (-40.9%) because long rationales break few-shot patterns.
agent_test: Test abduce-then-execute with and without answer options at equal tokens.

claim: Execution-checked rule programs help: LLM-written Prolog rules with failing-step feedback reach 88.6% on I-RAVEN-X vs 34% direct; Python repair 81.6% vs 64% direct. Real feedback beats generic hints (corrective hints up to +100% relative; general hints hurt).
agent_test: Add code-execution check of a stated rule against the given cells; compare with self-critique alone.

claim: Training on rule patterns gives in-distribution gains but not transfer: fine-tuned LLaMA2 0.977 in-distribution, near chance on compositional splits; Qwen2-VCog 70% in-distribution, RAVEN OOD 29-32%; SCL 89% on RAVEN falls to 62-68% on hand-made concept variations; auxiliary rule loss is inconsistent (RAVEN: hurt; PGM: helped).
agent_test: Judge scaffold gains on shifted layouts and concept variations, not only the original test set.

claim: The GPT-3 analogical-reasoning claim is contested: Webb 2023 found GPT-3 above students on Digit Matrices (OR 1.88 generative, 6.27 MC) and letter strings, but counterfactual versions (permuted alphabets) keep humans high while GPT-3, 3.5 and 4 drop; GPT-4 with code execution matches humans in the reply.
agent_test: Test the agent on counterfactual variants of a rule task (shuffled symbols) at equal tokens.

claim: High-scoring humans use constructive matching (study matrix first, then options) and adapt strategy with difficulty; wrong answers shift from repetition errors (low ability) to incomplete-correlate errors (higher ability).
agent_test: Require the agent to commit to a predicted cell before options are shown; compare with options-first.

claim: Working-memory capacity links more strongly to harder Raven items once the overall WM-Raven correlation is high enough; earlier flat results are explained by low overall correlation. Rule novelty added no effect (p = 0.39).
agent_test: Vary the number of rules held at once; check accuracy drop by difficulty.

claim: Working-memory training (dual n-back) did not transfer to matrix tests in a controlled replication (N=58).
agent_test: Shows practice on a surface task does not move the general skill; no direct agent test.

claim: Matrix tests are not a pure measure of g and have no special status; verbalising can interfere with visual items (DeShon 1995). Only secondary mentions were read.
agent_test: Not testable until primary sources are read.

claim: Format sensitivity is large in NeuroCognition (multiple choice vs generative swings of -0.175 to +0.065 per model), but RAPM was run once per model, so run-to-run variance for format and for reasoning on/off is unmeasured. Humans (N=9, each did both) showed no consistent format direction. Run-to-run SD is known only for spatial memory (up to 0.38) and for ConceptARC rule labels (about 2/3 agreement).
agent_test: Run each item with 3 seeds and both answer formats; report SD.

claim: LLM failure patterns on Raven: invented visual features, over-clever rules that skip simple local rules (XOR, concatenation), answers that satisfy only part of the evidence; reasoning text is often unfaithful to the answer (GPT-4V 50%, Gemini 25%).
schema_part: check answer against all rows and columns
agent_test: Add a step that checks the chosen answer against every row and column rule; measure partial-match errors.

claim: Woodcock-Johnson Concept Formation is inductive rule discovery from instances and non-instances with frequent rule switching; Analysis-Synthesis is sequential/deductive rule application with a key. Both load on one fluid-reasoning factor with Matrix Reasoning (all standardised loadings above .65, N=69 children) but are modest g measures (WJ IV Schmid-Leiman g loadings .50-.56, so 25-32% of variance). No LLM study on either test was found.
agent_test: Open the WJ manuals; analogue is rule discovery from feedback.

claim: Making the model predict the missing panel first and then match it to options by code beats showing options and asking it to pick, on the leak-free I-RAVEN centre set: GPT-4 74.8% vs 56.0-60.0%, Llama-3 70B 79.0% vs 22.4-22.8%. Not matched on tokens and no options-only control, so the constructive-matching advantage is promising, not proven for our agent.
agent_test: On our items, run option-hidden predict-then-match vs options-visible, equal token cap, plus an options-only control; keep the predict-first arm only if it wins and the control stays at chance.

claim: The arithmetic-rule weakness is partly rule induction (32 of 68 GPT-4 arithmetic errors fit a rule inferred from the last row only) and partly range handling (arithmetic below 10% at range 1000 without tools). Reasoning models without tools reach 60.8-65.8% at range 1000. No calculator or code arm has been tested.
agent_test: Run ranges 100 and 1000 with and without a code tool and with a force-use-first-two-rows step; compare arithmetic-rule accuracy.

claim: Reasoning models pay about 5,000-19,000 output tokens per I-RAVEN item (o3-mini medium 5,445-7,209; high 9,867-19,449; R1 4,486-6,324) against about 21 tokens for a prompted GPT-4. More effort did not help on the hardest setting, so token cap plus verification is the better budget rule.
agent_test: Log tokens per item for each arm; plot accuracy against tokens before choosing a cap.

claim: No LLM study has tested keeping several candidate rules alive on matrices. The only supporting evidence is a trained model that combines all rules by confidence-weighted soft selection (ARLC 88.0% under the same uncertainty where LLMs fall to 17-23%), with no ablation isolating the multi-rule part.
agent_test: Compare single-rule commit vs top-3 rules with weights under confounders and smoothed values; measure the drop from the clean setting.

claim: Naming the rule type does not reliably help: LLM pattern hints had no significant mean effect (p=.18, .45, .67), and in RAVEN an added rule-classification loss hurt one network (59.56% to 20.71%) and left another unchanged. Where rule labels help (PGM +13.9) the setting differs.
agent_test: Do not add a name-the-rule step without an ablation; test rule execution checks instead.

claim: Accuracy overstates competence: about 27% of o3's correct ConceptARC text answers rested on unintended or wrong rules (humans about 7%), and rule labels agree across repeats only about two thirds of the time. Python tools helped images (5.6% to 29.2% for o3) but not text (77.1% to 75.6%).
agent_test: Score the stated rule as well as the answer; repeat 3 times and require stable rule labels.

claim: Memorisation on matrices for current models is untested. Counterfactual work covers letter strings with GPT-3 to GPT-4 (Hodel and West; Lewis and Mitchell), not Raven-style items with 2025-26 reasoning models, and the Webb et al. reply (code execution fixes counting errors) is unresolved. Trained transformers fall to 31-47% on rules left out of training.
agent_test: Run the same rules under re-labelled symbols and shuffled orders on current models, with and without code, and compare.
